findings.text: The opening paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves ("AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable"). That answers 'what is it' and 'why it matters' right away.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository.

findings.text: Someone arriving at the Athena site gets one paragraph about Athena, and the rest of the page studies a different project, firstmate. The second paragraph explains why the study is there, but a newcomer may still be unsure whether they are on Athena's home page or a sample of its output.

The page never shows these Athena features in action. Nothing in the study says which model wrote it, which one checked it, what it cost, or what verdict it got. A newcomer has to take the main selling points on trust.
findings.source: It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: the repo link, the clone command, the prerequisites (git 2.40+, a C linker, curl, Claude Code or npm), `./setup.sh`, and a sample `athena ask "add a changelog"`. The header links straight to this section, so 'what do I do next' is answered well.
A newcomer is not an owner. Putting this link in the header with no explanation of who the owner is, or what proposals they decide on, may confuse a first-time reader.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The 'Start here' section works well. It says in one sentence what firstmate is, defines terms before using them, follows one task from start to finish, and lists failure cases and missing limits. Someone who never reads further still leaves with a clear picture.

The twelve transition cards are dense: exit codes, pending-close records, `mode=retain`, harness pins. They also repeat much of 'Start here'. This detail is too heavy for a newcomer, though a careful reader can still follow it.
The early term list repeats Glossary entries almost word for word ('See the Glossary entry for captain'). This makes the page longer without helping a newcomer.

The limits section is candid: nothing was run, and a first pass missed several paths. That honesty helps trust. But a newcomer judging Athena may read it as a sign that Athena's studies are incomplete.
findings.source: f3 ... A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths

findings.text: This section points to a `studies/` folder that a newcomer has never seen, so it means nothing to them on this page.
